cards.name: Poison ivy (plant contact dermatitis)
short: Urushiol, an oily liquid from the plant, enters the skin within 10 minutes.
Blisters in a line where the plant brushed the skin; rash 2–48 hours later, lasting 1–3 weeks.
Refer at 7 days without improvement, or with the face, eyelids or genitalia involved.
Itching: oral antihistamine. Weeping: aluminum acetate.
Not used: topical antihistamines and topical antibiotics.

steps.title: Cause and timing
steps.q: How fast does urushiol enter the skin, when does the rash appear, and how long does it last?

rows: [[urushiol|Urushiol]], the {{oily liquid}} in poison ivy, oak and sumac; the active irritant
{{50 to 70%}} of people are sensitive; sensitivity tends to run in families
Within {{10 minutes}} of contact; it binds epidermal proteins to form an antigen
Dead, dried plants and contaminated objects, for {{several years}}
Hands and objects, which carry it to other parts of the body
{{Pets}}, which often carry it to people
Protective clothing and gloves when working outside near vegetation

steps.title: Recognize it
steps.q: What do the early lesions look like, and in what order do the symptoms appear?

rows: Multiple small blisters ([[vesicle|vesicles]]) {{in a line}} where the skin brushed the plant
Inhaling smoke from burning poison ivy, oak or sumac can cause {{severe respiratory symptoms}}

steps.title: Self-care, or refer?
steps.q: Name the five reasons to refer.

items: ★ No improvement after {{7 days}}
Symptoms become worse
Rash covers a large area of the {{face}}, or the {{eyelids}} swell
Rash involves the {{genitalia}}
{{Secondary infection}}

rows: Symptoms can last up to {{3 weeks}}

steps.title: Treat it: match the product to the symptom
steps.q: What do you give for itching, what for weeping, and which two products are not used?
steps.src: Patel Outdoor slides 9, 11–15; 11/12 lecture and polls

blocks.label: Just exposed
blocks.title: Remove the urushiol as soon as possible
pts: Rinse with {{large volumes of water}}
Then wash with soap and water, including {{under the nails}}
Other agents: Tecnu, Zanfel, Dial Ultra dishwashing soap

blocks.label: Itching
blocks.title: Oral antihistamine or colloidal oatmeal bath
pts: ★ Her poll answer: an {{oral antihistamine}} (the option was diphenhydramine 25 mg by mouth; "any oral antihistamine is appropriate")
Oatmeal bath: soak {{15–20 minutes}} twice daily, pat the skin dry
Cool soaks or baths
blocks.warn: Not used for plant dermatitis: <<topical-antihistamine|topical antihistamines>> and <<topical-antibiotics|topical antibiotics>>.

blocks.label: Wet or weeping
blocks.title: Astringent
pts: ★ Her poll answer: {{aluminum acetate}} (Burow's solution), an [[astringent|astringent]], as a {{soak or wet dressing}}
Aluminum sulfate/calcium acetate is used the same way
Hydrocortisone is listed for wet or dry plant dermatitis

blocks.label: Dry rash
blocks.title: Topical products
pts: Hydrocortisone: wet or dry rash; not for a child under {{2 years}}
Topical anesthetics: dry rash only; not on {{broken skin}} or under an occlusive dressing; adverse effect of the "caines": [[methemoglobinemia|methemoglobinemia]]
[[counterirritant|Counterirritants]] such as camphor or menthol: dry rash only; not on broken skin or a wound
pick: No topical anesthetic and no counterirritant

blocks.label: Severe
blocks.title: Oral corticosteroids
pts: Topical corticosteroids suit any presentation; oral corticosteroids are for severe cases
blocks.move: Refer when: no improvement after 7 days, worse, face or eyelids, genitalia, or infection.

blocks.label: Reference table: plant dermatitis by symptom

patients.t: A woman hiked through poison ivy 2 days ago. Her legs and ankles have closed vesicles and papules on red skin, with no weeping. She says the itching will not stop. She takes lisinopril for hypertension.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: The complaint is itching, and itching is treated with an oral antihistamine (her poll; any oral antihistamine is appropriate).

x.An aluminum acetate soak: Aluminum acetate treats weeping, and the exam found no weeping.
x.A topical antihistamine: Topical antihistamines are not used for plant dermatitis.
x.Referral to a physician: None of the five referral reasons is present 2 days into the rash.

patients.t: The same patient returns 2 days later. The vesicles have opened and the rash on her ankles is weeping.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: Aluminum acetate, as a soak or wet dressing, reduces weeping (her second poll).

x.An oral antihistamine: An oral antihistamine treats itching; it does not dry a weeping rash.
x.A topical antihistamine: Topical antihistamines are avoided in plant dermatitis and on broken, oozing skin.
x.Referral to a physician: Weeping by itself is treated with an astringent; no referral reason is given.

patients.t: A man cleared brush 3 days ago. A dry, itchy rash now covers much of his face, and both eyelids are swollen.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: A rash over a large area of the face, or swelling of the eyelids, is a reason to refer.

x.An oral antihistamine: It treats itching, but the face and eyelids make this patient a referral.
x.An aluminum acetate soak: The rash is dry, and the face and eyelids make this patient a referral.
x.A topical antihistamine: Topical antihistamines are not used for plant dermatitis.

patients.t: A patient has used hydrocortisone cream and oatmeal baths on a poison ivy rash on the forearm for 8 days. The rash looks the same.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: No improvement after 7 days is a reason to refer.

x.An oral antihistamine: Self-care has passed 7 days without improvement.
x.An aluminum acetate soak: Self-care has passed 7 days without improvement, and no weeping is described.
x.A topical antihistamine: Topical antihistamines are not used for plant dermatitis.

patients.t: A mother asks for a cream for her 18-month-old son, who has a dry, closed poison ivy rash on one forearm that itches.
patients.q: Which product class is ruled out by his age?
patients.w: Her chart says not to use topical hydrocortisone on a child under 2 years old.

x.Colloidal oatmeal bath: Her slide gives no age limit for the oatmeal bath.
x.Cool soaks: Cool soaks or baths are a non-drug measure with no age limit on her slide.
x.Aluminum acetate soak: Her slides give no age limit for the astringent soak.

patients.t: A man touched poison ivy while gardening 5 minutes ago. His skin looks normal.
patients.q: What should he do first?
o: Apply hydrocortisone cream to the area
Rinse with large volumes of water
patients.w: Urushiol enters the skin within 10 minutes, so it is removed as soon as possible: large volumes of water, then soap and water including under the nails.

x.Apply hydrocortisone cream to the area: Hydrocortisone treats itch and inflammation once a rash appears; it does not remove urushiol.
x.Take an oral antihistamine tablet: An oral antihistamine treats itching; there is none yet, and it does not remove urushiol.
x.Apply a topical antibiotic ointment: Topical antibiotics are not used for plant dermatitis.

numbers: rash continues; resolves with or without treatment
of people are sensitive to urushiol
urushiol stays active on dead plants and objects

cards.name: Insect bites
short: Bites are nonvenomous: mosquitoes, fleas, bedbugs, ticks, chiggers, most spiders.
Local effects: mild pruritus, erythema, papules.
Self-care for at most 7 days; refer if worse, infected, or a vector-borne disease is suspected.
Any one or a combination: skin protectant, hydrocortisone, topical anesthetic, counterirritant, oral antihistamine.
Under 2 years: a skin protectant; no hydrocortisone, local anesthetic or counterirritant.

steps.title: Cause and prevention
steps.q: Which insects bite, which of them carry disease, and how are bites prevented?

rows: Use an insect repellent (she will not ask the ingredients)
Cover the skin; cuff pant legs into socks
Avoid habitat areas; keep pets free of pests
Remove standing water and wood piles

steps.title: Recognize it
steps.q: What are the local effects of a bite?

rows: Pain with venom and allergenic proteins is a sting (bees, wasps, yellow jackets, hornets, fire ants)

steps.title: Self-care, or refer?
steps.q: What is the self-care limit, and which findings send the patient to a physician?

items: ★ Symptoms persist after {{7 days}} of treatment (her poll: the maximum self-care duration is seven days)
Symptoms {{worsen}} during treatment
Secondary infection: {{fever}}, {{joint pain}}, {{lymph node enlargement}}, neurologic symptoms
A vector-borne disease is suspected: refer to the prescriber

steps.title: Treat it: match the product to the situation
steps.q: Which non-drug steps come first, which products may be used, and what changes under 2 years?
steps.src: Patel Outdoor slides 12–13, 24–25, 39–40; 11/12 lecture and polls

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: Non-drug measures
pts: Apply an ice pack promptly: less swelling, itching and pain
Avoid scratching; keep fingernails trimmed
No rough, irritating clothing over the bite

blocks.label: Tick attached
blocks.title: Remove it with tweezers
pts: Grasp the tick's {{head}} and pull gently; remove the head
Clean the skin with {{rubbing alcohol}}
Keep the tick in a {{plastic bag}}

blocks.label: Itching
blocks.title: Any one or a combination
pts: ★ Her bedbug poll: {{oral diphenhydramine}} for the itch
Hydrocortisone treats pruritus and inflammation
Topical anesthetics (pramoxine, benzocaine) and [[counterirritant|counterirritants]] (camphor, menthol): {{3–4 times daily}}, not longer than {{7 days}}
Her chart also lists topical diphenhydramine 0.5 to 2% for bites and stings
pick: No Neosporin; a <<topical-antibiotics|topical antibiotic>> does not treat itch
An [[astringent|astringent]], used for wet or weeping dermatitis
No topical antihistamine, anesthetic or counterirritant

blocks.label: Under 2 years
blocks.title: Skin protectant
pts: ★ [[skin-protectant|Skin protectants]] (petrolatum, calamine, zinc oxide) can be used under {{2 years}}
As needed, up to {{4 times daily}}
blocks.warn: Under 2 years: no hydrocortisone, no local anesthetic, no counterirritant.

blocks.text: Do not use hydrocortisone on scabies, bacterial infections or fungal infections: steroids can mask or worsen them.

blocks.label: Reference table: insect bites and stings

patients.t: A 23-year-old man has bedbug bites on his lower legs and torso after a hotel stay. The bites are very itchy. He takes no medications and is allergic to neomycin, which worsened a rash.
patients.q: Which product is the most appropriate for the itching?
o: No product; refer to the physician
patients.w: Her poll answer: oral diphenhydramine treats the pruritus.

x.Witch hazel: Witch hazel is an astringent, for wet or weeping dermatitis.
x.Neosporin ointment: It contains neomycin, his allergy, and a topical antibiotic does not treat itch.
x.No product; refer to the physician: He has local symptoms only and no referral finding.

patients.t: A mother asks what she can put on mosquito bites on her 14-month-old daughter's arms. The bites are small red papules.
patients.q: Which product can be used at this age?
patients.w: Skin protectants (petrolatum, calamine, zinc oxide) can be applied under 2 years.

x.Hydrocortisone 1% cream: Hydrocortisone is not used on a child under 2 years old.
x.Benzocaine spray: Local anesthetics are not used on children younger than 2 years.
x.Camphor and menthol lotion: Counterirritants are not used on children younger than 2 years.

patients.t: A man has used pramoxine cream 3 times daily on flea bites on his ankles for 8 days. The itching is unchanged.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: Symptoms that persist after 7 days of treatment are referred, and local anesthetics are not used longer than 7 days.

x.Continue pramoxine for 7 more days: Local anesthetics are not used longer than 7 days.
x.Change to benzocaine: Another local anesthetic does not reset the 7-day self-care limit.
x.Add a camphor product: Counterirritants also stop at 7 days, and persistent symptoms are referred.

patients.t: A woman finds a tick attached to her calf after a hike and asks how to remove it.
patients.q: What do you tell her?
o: Squeeze the body with the fingers
Scrape it off with a card edge
Cover it with petrolatum and wait
Pull it out by the head with tweezers
patients.w: Her slide: remove ticks with tweezers by grasping the head and gently pulling; remove the head, clean with rubbing alcohol, keep the tick in a plastic bag.

x.Squeeze the body with the fingers: Her slide says tweezers on the tick's head.
x.Cover it with petrolatum and wait: This is not on her slide; the tick is removed with tweezers.
x.Scrape it off with a card edge: A card was the mother's method for a bee stinger in her sting case, not for a tick.

patients.t: A man was bitten by chiggers 4 days ago. He now has a fever and enlarged lymph nodes in the groin.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: Fever and lymph node enlargement are signs of secondary infection on her follow-up slide: refer.

x.Hydrocortisone 1% cream: It treats local itch and inflammation; fever and lymph nodes need a physician.
x.Oral diphenhydramine: It treats itching; fever and lymph nodes need a physician.
x.Calamine lotion: A skin protectant does not address fever and lymph node enlargement.

numbers: maximum self-care; persistent symptoms are referred
no hydrocortisone, local anesthetic or counterirritant

cards.name: Flea-borne and tick-borne disease
short: Fleas: murine typhus (Texas) and bubonic plague (Southwest U.S.). Ticks: Lyme disease, rickettsial spotted fevers.
Flu-like symptoms and a rash days after exposure: not self-care; immediate medical referral.
Murine typhus and rickettsial fevers: doxycycline.
Lyme prophylaxis: one dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of detaching the tick.
Erythema migrans: doxycycline 10 days, amoxicillin 14, cefuroxime axetil 14, azithromycin 7 (second line).

steps.title: Cause and timing
steps.q: Which vector and place go with each disease, and how long after exposure do symptoms start?

rows: Rickettsia typhi; {{fleas}}; {{Texas}}; carriers cats, rodents, opossums; incubation {{6 to 14 days}}
Yersinia pestis; fleas; {{Southwest U.S.}}; carriers rodents, pet cats and dogs
Lyme disease, rickettsial spotted fevers, tularemia, ehrlichiosis; symptoms {{2 to 14 days}} after the bite

steps.title: Recognize it
steps.q: What does murine typhus look like, and what are the tick-borne symptoms?

rows: {{5 or 6 days}} later: a rash that starts on the {{trunk}} and spreads to the arms and legs
Untreated, it may last several months

steps.title: Self-care, or refer?
steps.q: What did she answer for the hunter with muscle aches and a leg rash?

items: ★ Her hunter poll: flu-like symptoms, muscle aches and a leg rash about 10 days after a hunting trip: {{immediate medical referral}}
Her cues: the duration and the symptoms
If a [[vector|vector-borne]] disease is suspected, refer to the {{prescriber}}
{{Fever}}, joint pain, lymph node enlargement or neurologic symptoms after a bite: refer

blocks.text: Not self-care: a suspected vector-borne disease is referred.

steps.title: Treat it: which antibiotic for which disease
steps.q: Which antibiotic treats murine typhus, and what are the Lyme prophylaxis window and the four treatment durations?

blocks.title: Antibiotic by disease ("it's bolded for a reason"; she does not ask the flea-borne doses)
rows: Streptomycin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, doxycycline, aminoglycosides
Doxycycline, 7 days; recommended for all suspected rickettsial infections

blocks.label: Lyme: after the bite
blocks.title: Prophylaxis
pts: ★ Prophylaxis is given within {{72 hours}} of detaching the tick ("pay attention to the hour")
Doxycycline 200 mg by mouth {{once}}; children 4.4 mg/kg up to 200 mg once

blocks.label: Lyme: skin lesion
blocks.title: Erythema migrans (early localized disease)
pts: ★ Doxycycline 100 mg BID for {{10 days}}
★ Amoxicillin 500 mg TID for {{14 days}}
★ Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg BID for {{14 days}}
★ Second line: azithromycin 500 mg daily for {{7 days}}

blocks.label: Lyme: later
blocks.title: Neurologic, cardiac, arthritic
pts: Neurologic: IV ceftriaxone, penicillin G or oral doxycycline, 14 to 21 days
Cardiac: hospitalized, IV ceftriaxone; not hospitalized, an oral agent, 14–21 days
Arthritic: oral antibiotics for 28 days

blocks.label: Reference table: antibiotic by flea-borne and tick-borne disease

patients.t: A 24-year-old man asks for something for flu-like symptoms. He has felt ill with muscle aches for a couple of days, and a rash appeared on his leg several days after he returned from a hunting trip to Minnesota about 10 days ago. Two days of rest and fluids have not helped.
patients.q: What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: An OTC cold and flu product
patients.w: Her poll answer. The time since the trip, the muscle aches and the rash point to a tick-borne disease.

x.An OTC cold and flu product: The rash after outdoor exposure makes a vector-borne disease likely; OTC products do not treat it.
x.Monitor for 3 to 5 more days: Symptoms have already persisted; a suspected vector-borne disease is referred at once.
x.No action is needed: Muscle aches with a rash after a hunting trip need medical care.

patients.t: A woman in a high endemic area removed a black-legged tick 1 day ago. It had been attached for about 2 days. She has no symptoms.
patients.q: Which regimen on her slide fits this patient?
patients.w: All three high-risk criteria are met and she is within 72 hours of detaching the tick: prophylaxis is one 200 mg dose of doxycycline.

x.Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 10 days: That is the treatment of erythema migrans; she has no lesion.
x.Amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 14 days: That is a treatment regimen for erythema migrans, not prophylaxis.
x.Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 7 days: That is the second-line treatment for erythema migrans.

patients.t: A man in Texas has had headache, fever, nausea and body aches for 6 days. A rash started on his trunk and is spreading to his arms and legs. His cats have fleas.
patients.q: Which antibiotic does her slide list for this disease?
patients.w: This is murine typhus (flea-borne, Texas, rash from the trunk outward 5 or 6 days after the first symptoms); her slide lists doxycycline.

x.Amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is on her slide for erythema migrans of Lyme disease.
x.Cefuroxime axetil: Cefuroxime axetil is on her slide for erythema migrans of Lyme disease.
x.Azithromycin: Azithromycin is the second-line agent for erythema migrans.

patients.t: A prescriber diagnoses erythema migrans in an adult and chooses amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily.
patients.q: For how many days is it given?
patients.w: Amoxicillin and cefuroxime axetil are each given for 14 days.

x.7 days: 7 days is azithromycin, the second-line agent.
x.28 days: 28 days is oral antibiotics for arthritic manifestations.

patients.t: A patient has a rash after a Lone Star tick bite, and the prescriber diagnoses southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI).
patients.q: What does her slide say about antibiotics?
patients.w: Her slide: STARI, Lone Star tick, IDSA: no antibiotic recommendation.

x.Doxycycline 200 mg once: That is Lyme prophylaxis after an Ixodes tick bite.
x.Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days: That is the regimen for rickettsial spotted fevers.
x.Amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 14 days: That is a regimen for erythema migrans.

numbers: Lyme prophylaxis window after detaching the tick
tick attachment that makes Lyme risk high
doxycycline prophylaxis, adults (children 4.4 mg/kg up to 200 mg)
azithromycin (second line); doxycycline for rickettsial spotted fevers
typhus rash after the first symptoms

cards.name: Insect stings
short: Stings are venomous and contain allergenic proteins: bees, wasps, yellow jackets, hornets, fire ants.
Local effects: pain, pruritus, irritation.
Hives, dizziness, nausea or vomiting, difficulty breathing, or a severe reaction history: emergency care immediately.
First aid: remove the stinger without squeezing, soap and water, ice.
Same drug treatment as bites; an oral analgesic if a topical does not relieve the pain.

steps.title: Cause
steps.q: Which insects sting, and what makes a sting different from a bite?

steps.title: Recognize it
steps.q: What are the local effects of a sting?

rows: A swollen, bright red patch on the thigh that hurts and itches

steps.title: Self-care, or emergency?
steps.q: Which findings mean emergency care immediately, and when is the patient triaged to a provider?

items: {{Severe reaction history}}
★ At any time after the sting: {{hives}}, {{dizziness}}, nausea or vomiting, {{difficulty breathing}}
★ Her poll: a wasp or bee sting with hives and swelling: {{immediate referral to the emergency room}}
Symptoms worsen or do not improve after {{7 days}} of topical treatment

steps.title: Treat it: first aid, then the product
steps.q: What are the first-aid steps, and what is added when a topical does not relieve the pain?

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: First aid
pts: Remove the bee stinger and venom sac ({{do not squeeze it}}) before all the venom is injected
Wash the area with {{soap and water}}
Apply {{ice or a cold pack}}: slows absorption, reduces pain and swelling
Clean with rubbing alcohol; avoid scratching; no rough clothing over the area

blocks.label: Pain and itching
blocks.title: Same drug treatment as insect bites
pts: Local anesthetics and [[counterirritant|counterirritants]]: {{3–4 times daily}}, not longer than 7 days
Pramoxine or benzyl alcohol: less likely to cause [[sensitization|sensitization]] or adverse effects
pick: [[skin-protectant|Skin protectant]] (zinc oxide, calamine); no hydrocortisone, anesthetic or counterirritant

blocks.label: Pain not relieved
blocks.title: Oral analgesic
pts: If a topical does not relieve the pain, consider an {{oral analgesic}}

blocks.label: Reference table: insect bites and stings

patients.t: A 7-year-old boy was stung on the thigh near a creek, where he saw flying yellow and black insects. His mother removed the stinger and applied ice. The thigh is swollen and bright red, and hives have developed away from the sting site. He has asthma and takes loratadine and montelukast.
patients.q: What is the best option?
o: Soak the area in an Epsom salt bath
Apply a local topical anesthetic to the area
Immediate referral to the emergency room
patients.w: Her poll: "Keyword here, hives and swelling." Hives at any time after a sting mean emergency care immediately.

x.Apply a local topical anesthetic to the: It treats local pain; hives away from the site are an emergency sign.
x.Apply a topical antihistamine cream: A cream on the sting site does not manage a systemic reaction.
x.Soak the area in an Epsom salt bath: Not on her slides, and hives are an emergency sign.

patients.t: A 30-year-old woman was stung on the forearm by a wasp 20 minutes ago. The site is painful, red and itchy. She has no hives, dizziness or trouble breathing and has never reacted severely to a sting.
patients.q: What do you recommend first?
o: Soap and water, then an ice pack
Go to the emergency room now
patients.w: A local reaction with no emergency sign is self-care: soap and water, then ice or a cold pack to slow absorption and reduce pain and swelling.

x.Go to the emergency room now: She has no emergency sign and no severe reaction history.
x.Start an oral antibiotic: Antibiotics are not part of sting first aid on her slide.
x.Apply a warm compress: Her slide uses ice or a cold pack.

patients.t: A man was stung by a bee an hour ago. He washed the area and has applied benzocaine and ice, and the pain is still not relieved. He has no hives, dizziness or trouble breathing.
patients.q: What does her slide add next?
patients.w: If pain is not relieved by a topical, consider an oral analgesic.

x.A topical antibiotic: Topical antibiotics are for minor burns and cuts.
x.A second topical anesthetic: The slide moves to an oral analgesic when a topical has not relieved the pain.
x.An astringent soak: Astringents are for wet or weeping dermatitis.

patients.t: A man asks for a product to keep at home for bee stings. Last summer a sting caused throat swelling and he was treated in an emergency room.
patients.q: What do you tell him about his next sting?
o: Apply ice and watch for 24 hours
Take an oral antihistamine and wait
patients.w: A severe reaction history is on her list for emergency care immediately.

x.Use hydrocortisone cream for 7 days: Self-care does not apply with a severe reaction history.
x.Take an oral antihistamine and wait: Waiting is not appropriate with a severe reaction history.
x.Apply ice and watch for 24 hours: Ice is first aid for a local reaction; his history makes any sting an emergency.

patients.t: A woman has used a camphor and menthol product on a hornet sting 3 times daily for 9 days. The area is still painful and swollen. She has no hives or trouble breathing.
patients.q: What do you recommend?
patients.w: Symptoms that do not improve after 7 days of topical treatment are triaged to a provider; counterirritants are not used longer than 7 days.

x.Continue for one more week: Counterirritants are not used longer than 7 days.
x.Switch to pramoxine: The 7-day limit has passed without improvement.
x.Go to the emergency room: She has none of the emergency signs; the slide triages her to a provider.

numbers: no improvement on topical treatment: triage to a provider
no local anesthetic or counterirritant; a protectant is allowed

cards.name: Lice (pediculosis)
short: Head lice are the most common: head-to-head contact or shared personal items; school children.
Self-care needs live lice seen and no exclusion (age, chrysanthemum or ragweed allergy, eyelids, pregnancy, infection).
OTC: pyrethrins + piperonyl butoxide (over 2 years), permethrin (over 2 months), dimethicone (over 2 months).
Dry hair, a full 10 minutes, rinse, nit comb in sections; repeat in 7 to 10 days if lice or nits are seen (slide 42: in 7 days).
Live lice after 2 rounds one week apart: refer for a prescription product.

steps.title: Cause: the three kinds
steps.q: Name the three kinds of lice, where each is found, and how each spreads.

rows: Pediculus humanus capitis; the {{most common}}; {{head-to-head contact}} or shared personal items; within {{4 mm}} (0.16 inch) of the scalp; mostly {{children in school}}
Pediculus humanus corporis; in the {{seams of clothing}}; can transmit {{typhus}} and trench fever
Phthirus pubis; pubic area; {{sexual contact}}, shared bedding or clothing
Kill adult and nymph lice; remove eggs ([[nit|nits]])

steps.title: Recognize it
steps.q: What did the mother in her case see?

rows: Itching with {{scratch marks}} on the scalp
Shared a helmet several days ago

steps.title: Self-care, or refer?
steps.q: List the exclusions for self-treatment, with the two age cut-offs.

items: {{No live lice}} seen
Hypersensitivity to {{chrysanthemums}}, {{ragweed}} or a [[pediculicide|pediculicide]] ingredient
Secondary skin infection in the infested area
★ Under {{2 years}} for pyrethrins (RID, A-200)
★ Under {{2 months}} for permethrin (Nix)
Lice of the {{eyelids or eyebrows}}
{{Pregnancy}} or breast-feeding
Active tumors
Live lice after {{2 treatment rounds}} one week apart: primary care provider, for a prescription product
Significant skin irritation, or product in the eyes: medical attention

steps.title: Treat it: pick the product by age, then counsel
steps.q: Give the age limit of each product, the time on the hair, and the steps of use.
steps.src: Patel Outdoor slides 43, 45–47; 11/12 lecture and poll

blocks.label: OTC
blocks.title: The three most common products
pts: ★ Her poll (10-year-old, live lice, no exclusion): first line {{permethrin}}
Permethrin (Nix Cream Rinse): over {{2 months}}
Pyrethrins + piperonyl butoxide (RID, A-200, Pronto): over {{2 years}}; chrysanthemum allergy
Dimethicone 100% (LiceMD): over 2 months
Each stays on the hair {{10 minutes}}

blocks.label: Other products
blocks.title: Ivermectin and the prescription agents
pts: Ivermectin lotion 0.5% (Sklice), OTC / Rx: over {{6 months}}; 10 minutes
Benzyl alcohol lotion 5% (Ulesfia), Rx: over 6 months; 10 minutes
Spinosad 0.9% (Natroba), Rx: over 6 months; 10 minutes
Malathion lotion 0.5% (Ovide), Rx: over 2 years; {{8–12 hours}}

blocks.label: How to use
blocks.title: Counseling steps
pts: No shampoo/conditioner combination or conditioner before the lice medicine
★ Apply enough to wet the {{dry}} hair and scalp
★ Leave on a full 10 minutes; rinse with water
★ Nit comb: part the hair into segments and comb each one
Do not re-wash the hair for 1–2 days

urushiol: The oily liquid in poison ivy, oak and sumac that causes the rash; the active irritant.
vesicle: A small blister; Dr. Patel’s slide writes “blisters (vesicles)”. Dr. Smith: in atopic dermatitis small, raised vesicles may leak fluid and crust over when scratched.
Patel Outdoor slide 10; Smith Pathophys slide 11
papule: A small, raised, solid bump on the skin. In acne (Dr. Patel): an inflammatory lesion, raised and red, with no visible pus.
Patel Acne slides 5–6; 11/10 lecture; the first sentence is the plain meaning
astringent: A product that reduces inflammation by vasoconstriction, cools and dries the skin, and slows oozing or weeping.
counterirritant: A topical antipruritic such as camphor or menthol that relieves pain and itching.
skin-protectant: A product such as zinc oxide, petrolatum, calamine or cocoa butter that gives the skin a physical barrier and lubrication and reduces irritation.
Patel Dermatitis slide 63; Outdoor slide 39; Sun slide 31
sensitization: The first exposure that makes the immune system react to a substance at later exposures.
methemoglobinemia: A condition in which the blood holds methemoglobin, a form of hemoglobin that carries oxygen poorly. Her slides list it as the adverse effect of the "caine" topical anesthetics; with benzocaine that is absorbed systemically: risk of cyanosis, dyspnea, syncope, seizures, coma.
Patel Outdoor slide 12; Wound slide 14; the first sentence is the plain meaning
vector: An insect that carries an infection to people; on her slide mosquitoes, fleas and ticks.
erythema-migrans: The acute skin lesion of early localized Lyme disease.
pep: Treatment given after an exposure to prevent the disease: for rabies, wound cleansing, vaccine and, if not previously vaccinated, immune globulin.
hrig: Human rabies immune globulin; her slides also write RHIG.
envenomation: Injection of venom by a bite or sting.
plain meaning, not from the slides

dry-bite: A snake bite that delivers no venom.
